narrative:
The model determined that you have a 39% chance of representing a bad credit risk. Because this probability exceeded the bank's acceptance threshold, your loan application was denied.

Three pieces of information about you weighed most heavily in this decision. The single biggest factor was your lack of savings. Most approved applicants have at least some money set aside; having no savings or an unknown amount pushed your prediction strongly toward higher risk. The second most important factor was the status of your checking account, which is currently none. While this is fairly common (about 59% of all applicants show no checking balance), in your specific combination of details it still contributed noticeably toward viewing you as higher risk. Finally, the loan amount you requested (DM 7,980) was substantially larger than the average amount approved applicants ask for (around DM 3,020). This larger sum pushed the prediction further toward bad credit.

Taken together, these three factors—your savings situation, checking-account status, and the size of the loan—were enough to tip the model against approval.

What you should do next is straightforward: build up visible savings, wait until you have a positive checking-account balance for several months, and then reapply for a smaller loan amount. These concrete changes tend to improve how models like this evaluate future applications.
